351.title: The dying man and the fire ordeal (6.15–6.16)
351.word: The dying man and the fire ordeal
351.hook: a family gathers around a dying man asking, do you know me? then an accused thief is handed a red-hot axe
351.howItsDone: Satya, truthfulness, is counted among the basic virtues in many Hindu ethical lists, including the yamas of the Yoga Sutras, and the Chandogya's closing lessons are often cited when teachers speak of truth as a protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: acharyavan, led home from the wilderness, village by village. Your line was someone points the way. Did you thank someone who once pointed for you? Week four of year two begins. Day three hundred fifty-one.

At a deathbed, there is a question families ask. They lean in close, and someone says, gently: do you know me? It's me. And for a while, the answer is yes, a squeeze of the hand, a name. And then, one day, it isn't. Uddalaka's last two lessons to his son begin at that bedside, and end somewhere very different: in a courtroom, ancient style, with an axe heating in a fire.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW ME? IT'S ME.` → `FOR A WHILE, YES.` → `AN AXE HEATING IN A FIRE.`

segments.voice: First, the bedside. When a man is very ill, Uddalaka says, his relatives gather and ask: do you know me? Do you know me? And as long as his speech hasn't gone into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and heat into the highest deity, he knows them. When it has, he doesn't. This is the creation story from ten days ago, running backward. Being became heat, water, food. At death, everything folds back, step by step, into Being. Then the second picture, and it's a hard one. In the ancient world, one way to test an accused person was an ordeal. Uddalaka describes it. They bring a man with his hands tied. He's taken something, they say. He's a thief. Heat the axe for him. If he did it, he makes himself false. Covering himself with untruth, he grips the hot axe, is burned, and is killed. If he didn't, he makes himself true. Covered with truth, he grips the axe, is not burned, and is set free. Hold this carefully. The Upanishad isn't teaching courtroom procedure, and nobody here is recommending an ordeal. It's using a picture its listeners knew to say one thing: a person wrapped in truth stands on what is real, and the fire can't reach him. A person wrapped in falsehood is standing on nothing. Then, for the last time, the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu. And the chapter ends with one quiet line: and he understood it. Yes, he understood. After all of his father's pictures, the son gets it.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW ME?` · `SPEECH INTO MIND, INTO BREATH, INTO BEING.` · `THE ACCUSED AND THE HOT AXE.` · `COVERED WITH TRUTH, NOT BURNED.` · then, large: `AND HE UNDERSTOOD IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice stands on what's true. Sit and settle. Notice a few simple true things: I'm breathing. I'm sitting here. My hands are warm or cool. Let each one be solid ground. Then notice if there's anything you've been holding that isn't quite true: a story you tell, a pretense, a small cover. You don't need to fix it now. Just notice how it feels to stand on it, and how it feels to stand on what's true. The bell holds the time.
The dying man and the fire ordeal. Uddalaka's last two lessons: everything folds back into Being at death, and one covered in truth is not burned.

segments.voice: Your line: truth protects. Today, in one small moment where a cover story would be easier, try the true one and see what happens. Day three hundred fifty-one.

352.title: Narada comes to Sanatkumara: "I know the Vedas — I don't know the Self" (7.1)
352.hook: the most learned sage in the room lists everything he has studied, then admits he is still in sorrow
352.howItsDone: Hindu traditions distinguish learning about scripture from knowledge of the self; many teachers quote Narada's confession to students who have studied much and still feel unsettled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dying man and the fire ordeal, the end of Uddalaka's lessons, and he understood it. Your line was truth protects. Did you try the true story instead of the easy one? Day three hundred fifty-two.

Every degree on the wall. Diplomas in three languages. A shelf of books with their name on the spine. People call for advice. And one night, the person who owns all of it sits down across from a friend and say, quietly: I know all this. And I'm not okay. The seventh chapter of the Chandogya opens with exactly that scene. The man with the diplomas is Narada, a famous sage, and the friend he goes to is the sage Sanatkumara.
screen: `EVERY DEGREE ON THE WALL.` → `I KNOW ALL THIS.` → `AND I'M NOT OKAY.`

segments.voice: Narada comes to Sanatkumara and says: teach me, sir. Sanatkumara answers: first tell me what you already know, and I'll teach you what's beyond it. So Narada recites his education, and it's a long list. The Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva as the fourth. The old stories and histories as a fifth Veda. Grammar. The rites for the ancestors. Mathematics. The reading of omens. The keeping of time. Logic. Ethics. The science of the gods, of the sacred word, of spirits, of weapons, of the stars, of serpents. Pretty much the whole library of his world. Then he says the honest sentence the chapter rests on. With all this, sir, I am only a knower of words. I am not a knower of the self. I have heard from people like you that the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow. In Sanskrit: tarati shokam atmavit. And I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say his learning was useless. It's real, and valuable, and it took a lifetime. He says it didn't do the one thing he needed. And Sanatkumara's first answer is startling: everything you've studied is only name. Then, over the next days, he'll lead Narada up a ladder, step by step, from name to something greater, and greater again. It's another of the Chandogya's great teacher-student dialogues. Uddalaka taught a proud son who thought he knew. Sanatkumara teaches a humble sage who knows he doesn't.
screen: `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW.` · `THE WHOLE LIBRARY OF HIS WORLD.` · `A KNOWER OF WORDS, NOT OF THE SELF.` · `ALL OF IT IS ONLY NAME.` · then, large: `TARATI SHOKAM ATMAVIT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice does what Narada did. Sit and settle. Quietly, in your mind, list what you know: your skills, your training, the things people come to you for. Let the list be long. Then, as honestly as Narada, notice what all of it hasn't touched: a sorrow, a restlessness, a question. Don't fix it. Just let it be said, the way he said it: and still, I'm in sorrow. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Atmavit, knower of the self. A sage who knows every subject, admitting he's a knower of words, not of the self, and asking to be taken across sorrow.
Your line: knowledge isn't it. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for one more fact to fix a feeling, pause and notice the feeling instead. Day three hundred fifty-two.

353.title: Name, speech, mind, will, thought — the ladder (7.1–7.5)
353.hook: Narada keeps asking one question, sir, is there anything greater than this? and every time, the answer is yes
353.howItsDone: Teachers of Vedanta often walk students up Sanatkumara's ladder as a contemplative exercise, moving attention from words to mind to awareness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atmavit, the learned sage who says I know only words, not the self. Your line was knowledge isn't it. Did you notice a feeling instead of reaching for a fact? Day three hundred fifty-three.

Kids discover a game early. Why? Because. But why? Because of this. But why that? It drives parents up the wall. And yet it's how you get to the bottom of things: you just keep asking for the next layer down. Sanatkumara has told Narada that everything he studied is only name. And Narada, to his credit, doesn't argue. He asks the next question. Sir, is there anything greater than name? And so begins the ladder.
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. BUT WHY?` → `ALL YOU KNOW IS ONLY NAME.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING GREATER?`

segments.voice: The first rung is name. Sanatkumara says: revere name as Brahman. As far as name reaches, you'll have freedom there. A fair start. Names are how we hold the world. Is there anything greater than name? Yes, speech is greater. Speech makes the Vedas known, and earth and sky, and right and wrong, true and false. If there were no speech, Sanatkumara says, right and wrong couldn't be made known at all. Is there anything greater than speech? Yes, mind. And here comes an image from the hand: as a closed fist holds two small fruits, mind holds both speech and name. When you think in your mind, let me learn these verses, then you learn them. Let me do this, then you do it. Greater than mind? Will, the Sanskrit samkalpa, intention. When you intend something, then you think it, then you say it, then you give it a name. Greater than will? Thought, citta, attention, the awareness that notices what's going on before you even intend. And Sanatkumara says something pointed here. If someone knows a great deal but has no real attention, people say: he's nobody. If someone knows little but is truly attentive, people want to listen. Look at the direction of the climb. Name, speech, mind, will, thought. Each rung is quieter and more inward than the last, and each one holds the one below it. Narada came in with a mountain of names. Sanatkumara is walking him up and in, toward the one who's paying attention. And at every rung, Narada asks again: is there anything greater?
screen: `NAME: HOW WE HOLD THE WORLD.` · `SPEECH: RIGHT AND WRONG MADE KNOWN.` · `MIND HOLDS BOTH, LIKE A FIST.` · `WILL, THEN THOUGHT.` · then, large: `EACH IS GREATER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice climbs the ladder inward. Sit and settle. Notice a name in your mind: anyone's, anything's. Then notice the inner voice that says it: speech. Then the mind behind the voice, where thoughts form. Then the intention under the thought, the pull toward something. Then the plain attention that notices all of it. Rest at that top rung, just noticing, for as long as you can. When you slip down, climb again. The bell holds the time.
Name. The first rung of Sanatkumara's ladder; above it, speech, mind, will and thought, each greater than the last.
Your line: each is greater. Today, before you say something important, notice the intention under it, the rung below the words. Day three hundred fifty-three.

354.title: Meditation, understanding, strength, food, water (7.6–7.10)
354.hook: the ladder climbs past thought to meditation, and then takes a surprising turn: toward strength, food and rain
354.howItsDone: Dhyana, meditation, is practiced across Hindu traditions, from Vedanta to yoga, where it is the seventh limb of Patanjali's eight; teachers often describe it with images of stillness like a mountain or a lamp in a windless place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: name, speech, mind, will, thought, the first rungs of Sanatkumara's ladder. Your line was each is greater. Did you notice the intention under your words? Day three hundred fifty-four.

If you were drawing a spiritual ladder, you'd probably make it climb from the body toward the mind, from the earthy to the airy. Lower things at the bottom, higher things at the top. Sanatkumara's ladder starts that way. Name, speech, mind, will, thought, each more inward. Then, today, it reaches meditation, the most inward step yet. And right after that, it does something nobody expects. It climbs toward a strong arm, a meal, and a rain cloud.
screen: `A LADDER FROM BODY TO MIND.` → `TODAY: MEDITATION.` → `THEN A STRONG ARM, A MEAL, A RAIN CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Greater than thought, Sanatkumara says, is meditation, dhyana. And his picture is beautiful. The earth meditates, as it were. The sky meditates, as it were. The waters, the mountains, gods and people, all meditate, as it were. Think of a mountain at dusk, utterly still. That stillness is what he means. He adds that people who achieve greatness seem to have a share of it, while small-minded people are quarrelsome and gossiping. Greater than meditation is understanding, vijnana: by it we know the Vedas, right and wrong, this world and the next. Then the turn. Greater than understanding is strength. One strong person, Sanatkumara says, can make a hundred people of understanding tremble. The earth stands by strength; the mountains stand by it. Greater than strength is food. Go without eating for ten days, and even if you live, you can't see or hear or think or understand. Remember Shvetaketu's fast? Same point. Food returns, and so do they. Greater than food is water. When the rains fail, people grow sick with worry about food; when the rains are good, they're glad. The earth, the sky, the mountains, people, animals, grass and trees, he says, are all just water in solid form. So what's going on? Why does the ladder climb into the body? One way to read it: Sanatkumara isn't ranking spirit over matter. He's asking what each thing depends on. Understanding depends on strength; strength on food; food on rain. The ladder climbs by asking what holds this up. And it keeps climbing.
screen: `THE EARTH MEDITATES, AS IT WERE.` · `UNDERSTANDING, THEN STRENGTH.` · `TEN DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` · `EARTH AND MOUNTAINS: WATER, MADE SOLID.` · then, large: `WHAT HOLDS THIS UP?`

segments.voice: Today's practice meditates the way a mountain does. Sit, and let your body settle like rock: heavy, still, supported by the ground. Don't try to do anything. A mountain doesn't try. Let the breath move on its own, like weather passing over a peak. Thoughts can come and go like clouds. You are just sitting, as the earth and the sky and the waters sit, meditating, as it were. The bell holds the time.
Meditation. Dhyana, the rung above thought: the stillness of earth, sky and mountains. Above it, understanding, strength, food and water.
Your line: the ladder climbs. Today, pick one thing you rely on, and ask what holds it up, and what holds that up. Day three hundred fifty-four.

355.title: Bhuman — the infinite, where one sees nothing else (7.23–7.24)
355.hook: at the top of the ladder Sanatkumara says it plainly: there's no happiness in the small; the infinite is happiness
355.tomorrow: the city of Brahman in the heart
355.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote 'the infinite is happiness; there is no happiness in the small' when distinguishing lasting joy from pleasure in possessions, and the bhuma-vidya is a standard topic in Vedanta study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: meditation, understanding, strength, food, water, the ladder asking what holds each thing up. Your line was the ladder climbs. What did you trace down to its support? Day three hundred fifty-five.

A kid swimming far out in the ocean on a summer afternoon. Friends at a table late at night, laughing until it hurts. A parent holding a newborn at 3am. Some people say afterward that in moments like these there was no thought of being happy. No one over here, and happiness over there. Just the thing itself. Sanatkumara's ladder, after many rungs, arrives at something like that, and gives it a name.
screen: `NO THOUGHT OF BEING HAPPY.` → `NO ONE OVER HERE.` → `JUST THE THING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Between yesterday and today, the ladder climbs through heat, space, memory, hope, and breath, and then turns toward truth, understanding, thinking, faith, steadfastness and action. And at the top Sanatkumara says: a person acts only when they find happiness. So, Narada, you should want to understand happiness. Then comes the line at the heart of the chapter. Yo vai bhuma tat sukham, nalpe sukham asti. The infinite is happiness. There is no happiness in the small. Bhuma means the vast, the full, the unbounded. Alpa means the small, the limited. And here's how you tell them apart: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the infinite. Where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else, that is the small. Think back to the ocean, the laughter, the newborn. Nothing else, for a moment. That's a taste of what he means. Narada asks a reasonable question: but sir, what does the infinite rest on? And Sanatkumara answers: on its own greatness. Or, not even on greatness. Then he explains what he doesn't mean. People here call cows and horses greatness, he says, and elephants and gold, servants and spouses, fields and houses. I don't mean that. Those things rest on something else. The infinite doesn't rest on anything. It's above and below, east and west, everywhere. And then he says: I am all this. The self is all this. The chapter ends quietly, saying Sanatkumara showed Narada the far shore beyond darkness.
screen: `WE ACT TO FIND HAPPINESS.` · `NO HAPPINESS IN THE SMALL.` · `WHERE ONE SEES NOTHING ELSE.` · `NOT COWS, GOLD OR HOUSES.` · then, large: `YO VAI BHUMA TAT SUKHAM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests in the wide. Sit and settle. Let your attention spread out: the sounds in the room, then beyond the room, then as far as you can hear. Let your sense of space open: above you, below you, on every side. Don't hold on to any one thing. When a thought pulls you into something small, notice it, and let the space open again. Just wide, and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Bhuman. The infinite, the vast: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else. There's no happiness in the small.
Your line: the infinite is happiness. Today, notice one moment when you get so absorbed that there's nothing else, and let it be enough. Day three hundred fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 355 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CITY OF BRAHMAN IN THE HEART.`

356.title: The city of Brahman in the heart (8.1)
356.hook: inside the body is a small lotus-shaped house, and inside that a small space, as big as all the space outside
356.tomorrow: Indra and Virochana learn from Prajapati
356.howItsDone: Meditation on the space in the heart, the dahara-vidya, is taught in several Hindu traditions, and many devotional schools picture God dwelling in the lotus of the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhuman, the infinite, where one sees nothing else. Your line was the infinite is happiness. Did you catch a moment with nothing else in it? Day three hundred fifty-six.

Russian nesting dolls get smaller as you go in. Open the big one, there's a smaller one. Open that, smaller again. Until you reach a tiny solid doll the size of a bean, and that's the end. The last chapter of the Chandogya opens with a nesting picture too, a city, a house, a room. Only this one does the opposite of what you'd expect. The farther in you go, the bigger it gets.
screen: `NESTING DOLLS, SMALLER EACH TIME.` → `A CITY, A HOUSE, A ROOM.` → `THE FARTHER IN, THE BIGGER.`

segments.voice: The eighth chapter begins: in this city of Brahman, there is a small house shaped like a lotus, and inside it a small space. What is inside that space is what should be sought, and understood. The city of Brahman is the body. The lotus-shaped house is the heart. And the small space is, well, small. So the students ask the obvious question. If there's a tiny space in a tiny house in this body, what could possibly be in there worth looking for? And the teacher answers: as large as this space out here is, that large is the space within the heart. Both heaven and earth are contained in it. Fire and wind, sun and moon, lightning and stars. Whatever there is here, and whatever there isn't, all of it is held there. Then the students push again, and it's a good question. If everything is held inside this body, what's left when the body grows old, or dies? The answer: that doesn't grow old when the body grows old. It isn't killed when the body is killed. That is the real city of Brahman. And the text describes that inner self: free from evil, from old age, from death, from grief, from hunger and thirst. Its desires are true. Its intentions are true. Remember the boy named Satyakama, the one who loves truth? Here the same word, satyakama, describes the self in every heart. So the nesting dolls run backward. Body, heart, a small space, and inside the small space, everything.
screen: `THE CITY, THE LOTUS, THE SMALL SPACE.` · `AS LARGE AS ALL THE SPACE OUTSIDE.` · `IT DOESN'T AGE WHEN THE BODY AGES.` · `ITS DESIRES ARE TRUE.` · then, large: `THE SPACE IN THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Today's practice goes in to go wide. Sit and settle. Bring your attention to the center of your chest. Breathe there for a few breaths. Imagine a small, quiet space there, like the inside of a closed flower. Then let that space open, gently, on each breath out: wider than your chest, wider than the room, as wide as the sky. Sun, moon and stars, held inside it. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Dahara, small, subtle. The body is the city, the heart a lotus-shaped house, and the small space inside holds heaven and earth.
Your line: the space in the heart. Today, when you feel crowded or small, put a hand on your chest and take one slow breath into that space. Day three hundred fifty-six.

357.title: Indra and Virochana learn from Prajapati — the body is not the self (8.7–8.8)
357.hook: a god and a demon study for thirty-two years, are told to look in a pan of water, and both walk away thinking the reflection is the self
357.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often use the story of Indra and Virochana to introduce the difference between the body and the self, and the story's stages are read as a step-by-step inquiry into who we are.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dahara, a small space as large as all space. Your line was the space in the heart. Did you breathe into it when things felt crowded? Today ends week four of year two. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

A mirror by the front door. Good shirt. Hair right. That's me, says the glance, before any thought. Then a selfie: me again. Then a tagged photo from ten years ago: somehow, also me. We point at a lot of pictures and say me. The Chandogya tells a story about two students who did exactly that, and one of them took the mistake home and built a whole philosophy on it.
screen: `GOOD SHIRT. HAIR RIGHT.` → `THAT'S ME.` → `WE POINT AT PICTURES AND SAY ME.`

segments.voice: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, announces: there is a self free from evil, from old age and death, from grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains all worlds. The gods and the demons both hear. The gods send their king, Indra. The demons send theirs, Virochana. The two rivals arrive with firewood in their hands, not speaking to each other, and live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati teaches them: the person seen in the eye, that is the self. Immortal, fearless. That is Brahman. They ask: and the one seen in water, or in a mirror? He says: it's seen in all these. Look at yourselves in a pan of water. They look. What do you see? Our whole selves, sir, down to the hair and the nails. Now dress up well, put on ornaments, and look again. They do. What do you see? Just as we are, sir, well dressed and adorned, so are these two. And Prajapati says: that is the self, immortal, fearless. Both leave content. Prajapati watches them go and says: they go without having found the self. Shankara and other commentators say Prajapati meant the seer behind the eye, and the students heard the image in the eye. Virochana goes home content and teaches the demons that the body is the self: honor it, adorn it, serve it. Indra sets off too. But on the road, something starts to bother him. Now the week, from the top. The fire ordeal, and truth protects. Narada, a knower of words. The ladder: name, speech, mind, will, thought. Meditation, strength, food, rain. The infinite. The space in the heart. And today, two students mistaking the reflection for the one who sees.
screen: `A SELF FREE FROM DEATH AND GRIEF.` · `THIRTY-TWO YEARS AS STUDENTS.` · `LOOK IN A PAN OF WATER.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE REFLECTION ISN'T YOU.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks past the reflection. Sit and settle. Picture your face in a mirror, as clearly as you can. Notice the details. Then ask, gently: who's looking? Not what's being seen, but the one seeing. Don't answer with words. Just turn your attention back toward the looking itself, like turning around in a doorway. Each time you drift back to the picture, turn around again. The bell holds the time.
Prajapati, lord of creatures. A god and a demon look in a pan of water, adorned, and both mistake the reflection for the self Prajapati described.
Your line: the reflection isn't you. Today, the next time you check a mirror or a photo of yourself, remember the one who is looking. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 357 COUNTS.` → `WEEK FOUR OF YEAR TWO, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: INDRA RETURNS.`

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: where they look for the self

myth: Indra and Virochana came together as friends
they came separately, not speaking to each other, rivals.
Prajapati says they go without having found the self
he watches them leave, satisfied with the reflection.
Virochana teaches the demons that the body is the self
he goes home content and teaches them to honor and adorn the body.

fork.setup: you're Indra. you've seen yourself, well dressed and adorned, in a pan of water, and Prajapati has said: that is the self. what do you do?
options: set off, but begin to have doubts on the road.
fork.reveal: Virochana goes home satisfied. Indra sets off too, but something starts to bother him, and tomorrow he comes back.

original.note: Sanskrit prajāpati: lord of creatures, the creator figure who teaches Indra and Virochana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a myth about gods and demons.
what it means: the first and easiest mistake about the self is to point at the body, the reflection, and say that's me.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 8.7–8.8; commentators read Prajapati's 'person seen in the eye' as the seer, which the students hear as the image in the pupil.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1–4 (Prajapati's proclamation; Indra and Virochana; thirty-two years; the person in the eye)
